## Latest JOLTS Report: Labor Market Remains Solid but Cooling

The most recent JOLTS data (August 2026) paints a picture of a labor market that is still healthy by historical standards but has moderated meaningfully from its post-pandemic peaks.

---

### Key Findings

- **Job Openings** came in at **7,079 thousand (about 7.1 million)** in August 2026 (JTSJOL, 2026-08-01), up **2.3% year-over-year** (JTSJOL, 2026-08-01) but down from a peak of **12,301 thousand** set in March 2022 (JTSJOL, 2022-03-01). Openings are now essentially in line with the 2019 average of **7,154 thousand** — just **1.0% below** that benchmark (JTSJOL, 2026-08-01).

- **Hiring Rate** held steady at **3.3%** in August 2026 (JTSHIR, 2026-08-01), within a narrow range of 3.1%–3.5% seen over the past two years, suggesting employers are filling roles at a consistent but unspectacular pace.

- **Quits Rate** edged down to **1.9%** in August 2026 (JTSQUR, 2026-08-01), near the low end of the recent range (1.9%–2.2%), indicating workers are becoming **less confident** about voluntarily leaving jobs — a sign of softening worker bargaining power.

- **Layoffs and Discharges** totaled **1,641 thousand** in August 2026 (JTSLDL, 2026-08-01), below the recent high of **1,891 thousand** in October 2025 (JTSLDL, 2025-10-01) and near the low end of the recent range, suggesting **no surge in involuntary separations**.

- **Historical context:** At 7,079 thousand, openings sit at the **68th percentile** of the past 20 years of data — higher than 68% of prior observations — and 48% of the way between the all-time low of **2,232 thousand** (July 2009) and the all-time high of **12,301 thousand** (March 2022) (JTSJOL, 2026-08-01).

---

### Bottom Line

The labor market is **normalizing, not collapsing**. Openings have returned to pre-pandemic levels, layoffs remain contained, but a declining quits rate signals that workers are growing more cautious — consistent with a gradual cooling rather than a sharp deterioration.

---

*Caveats: JOLTS data are subject to revision in subsequent releases. The series is released with approximately a one-month lag. A chart was produced showing job openings over the recent period.*

## Quits Rate: Minimal Decline Over the Past Year

The quits rate has been essentially flat over the past year, edging down only slightly. The most recent reading stands at **1.9%** (JTSQUR, 2026-08-01), down just **0.1 percentage points** from a year earlier (JTSQUR, 2026-08-01 change over 12 periods).

### Key Evidence:
- **Latest reading:** 1.9% in August 2026 (JTSQUR, 2026-08-01)
- **Year-over-year change:** −0.1 percentage points as of mid-2026, a trend consistent across April through August 2026 (JTSQUR, 2026-04-01 through 2026-08-01)
- **Range over the past 13 months:** The quits rate has fluctuated narrowly between **1.9% and 2.0%**, suggesting a period of relative stability at historically modest levels (JTSQUR, 2025-08-01 to 2026-08-01)
- **Longer-run context:** Over the full available window, the series ranged from a low of **1.9%** to a high of **2.3%**, with a mean of **2.04%** — the current rate sits at the bottom of that range (JTSQUR, 2023-10-01 to 2026-08-01)

### Takeaway:
Workers are quitting at a subdued and slowly declining pace, consistent with a cooling labor market where employees are less confident about finding new jobs.

---

> **Caveats:** JOLTS data are subject to revision. The latest observations may be preliminary and could be revised in subsequent releases.

## U.S. Job Openings: Peak and Current Level

Job openings **peaked in March 2022** at **12,301 thousand (about 12.3 million)**, and have since fallen significantly. As of **August 2026**, openings stand at **7,079 thousand (about 7.1 million)** — roughly **42% below the peak** (derived: (12,301 − 7,079) / 12,301 ≈ 42%).

### Key Evidence:
- **Peak:** 12,301 thousand in March 2022 (JTSJOL, 2022-03-01)
- **Latest reading:** 7,079 thousand in August 2026 (JTSJOL, 2026-08-01)
- **Pandemic trough:** The series hit a low of 4,606 thousand in April 2020 (JTSJOL, 2020-04-01), during the COVID-19 shock
- **Current position:** The August 2026 level sits only 32% of the way from that pandemic trough back up to the 2022 peak (JTSJOL, 2026-08-01)
- **Recent trend:** Openings fell 3.49% in August 2026 after a 2.13% gain in July 2026 (JTSJOL, 2026-07-01; JTSJOL, 2026-08-01), reflecting continued month-to-month volatility within a broader downtrend

### Caveats:
- JTSJOL is the **Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS)**, published by the BLS with an approximate **one-month lag** and subject to revision.
- Month-to-month swings can be noisy; the sustained decline from the 2022 peak is the more meaningful signal.

## 10-Year Treasury Yield: Historical Context

**Yes, the 10-year Treasury yield is elevated by recent standards, though it remains well below its all-time peak.**

### Key Facts

- **Current yield: 5.22%** as of October 8, 2026 (DGS10, 2026-10-08), in percent.
- **Higher than virtually all recent history:** Since October 2006, the yield ranks at the **100th percentile** — higher than 100% of the ~4,997 prior observations in that window (DGS10, 2026-10-08). The z-score of +2.12 confirms it is more than two standard deviations above the post-2006 mean of **2.89%** (DGS10, 2026-10-08).
- **Moderate vs. the full long-run record:** Looking back to 1962, the long-run mean is **5.80%** and the long-run median is not retrieved, so the current 5.22% is actually *below* the 64-year average (DGS10, 2026-10-08).
- **Far from the all-time high:** The record peak was **15.84%** on September 30, 1981 (DGS10, 1981-09-30), set during the Volcker-era inflation fight. The all-time low was **0.52%** on August 4, 2020 (DGS10, 2020-08-04). At 5.22%, the yield sits only **31% of the way** from that low to that high (DGS10, 2026-10-08).
- **Recent trend upward:** Over the past two weeks the yield has ranged from roughly **5.11% to 5.31%**, edging higher before the latest reading (DGS10, 2026-09-23 through 2026-10-08).

### Bottom Line

| Lens | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Post-2006 era | **Extremely high** (100th percentile) |
| Full history since 1962 | **Below the 64-year average of 5.80%** |
| Distance from all-time high | **Moderate** (31% of the min-to-max range) |

### Caveats
- Daily Treasury yields are subject to minor revisions. The post-2006 percentile rank reflects the prolonged low-rate era (2009–2022), so the "100th percentile" result is heavily shaped by that unusual period of near-zero rates.

A chart of the yield series was produced and is shown separately.

## Quits Rate: Not Quite Back to Pre-Pandemic Norms

**No, the quits rate has not fully returned to its pre-pandemic level — it remains below it.**

### Key Evidence

- **Current level:** The quits rate stands at **1.90%** (JTSQUR, 2026-08-01), seasonally adjusted.
- **2019 average:** The pre-pandemic baseline was **2.32%**, meaning today's rate is **0.42 percentage points (–18.0%) below** the 2019 average (JTSQUR, 2026-08-01 comparison).
- **Broader 2017–2019 average:** Even against the slightly lower 2017–2019 average of **2.24%**, the current rate is still **0.34 points (–15.3%) below** that benchmark (JTSQUR, 2026-08-01 comparison).
- **Pandemic-era peak:** The quits rate hit a record high of **3.00%** in November 2021 — the height of the "Great Resignation" — before declining sharply (JTSQUR, 2021-11-01).
- **Historical trough:** The all-time low in this series was **1.20%** in August 2009, during the Great Recession (JTSQUR, 2009-08-01). At 1.90%, the current rate sits only **39% of the way** from that trough to the 2021 peak.

### Caveats
- JOLTS data are subject to revision and carry a one-month release lag, so the August 2026 figure is preliminary.
- The quits rate is one dimension of labor market dynamism; other indicators (hiring, layoffs) may tell a somewhat different story.

A chart of this series was produced and is shown separately.

## Current Recession Risk Assessment

Both the Sahm Rule and the yield curve point to **low near-term recession risk** as of late 2026.

---

### Key Evidence

- **Sahm Rule: Not Triggered.** The indicator stands at **0.00 percentage points** (UNRATE-based, 2026-09-01), well below the 0.50 pp threshold that historically signals a recession is underway. It has been at zero for three consecutive months (July–September 2026).

- **Yield Curve: Positively Sloped (Normal).** As of 2026-10-08, the 10-year Treasury yields **5.22%** (DGS10, 2026-10-08) versus the 3-month at **4.23%** (DGS3MO, 2026-10-08), giving a **+0.99 pp 10y–3m spread** — a normal, upward-sloping curve. The 10y–2y spread is also positive at **+0.47 pp** (DGS10–DGS2, 2026-10-08).

- **Model-Based Recession Probability: 12%.** Using the Estrella & Trubin (NY Fed, 2006) probit model applied to the 10y–3m spread, the 12-month-ahead recession probability is **12%** (T10Y3M, 2026-10-31) — and has been **declining steadily** from 17% in June 2026 (2026-06-30) as the spread has widened.

- **Spread Trending More Positive.** The 10y–3m spread has widened from **+0.66 pp** (2026-06-30) to **+1.05 pp** (2026-10-31), consistent with diminishing inversion risk.

---

### Caveats

- The Sahm Rule is a **real-time recession signal**, not a leading indicator; it detects recessions already underway rather than predicting them.
- The yield curve model probability is **indicative only** and subject to revision as Treasury data is updated.
- Both series are subject to **data revisions**; the unemployment figures underlying the Sahm Rule may be revised.
- A chart of recent trends has been produced and is shown separately.

## Quits Rate vs. Unemployment Rate: Do They Move Together?

**No — they move in opposite directions, though the relationship is modest in magnitude.**

The correlation of *changes* in the quits rate (JTSQUR) and the unemployment rate (UNRATE) is **–0.29** over 306 overlapping observations from February 2001 to August 2026 (JTSQUR & UNRATE, 2001-02-01). This negative correlation means that when the quits rate rises, the unemployment rate tends to fall, and vice versa — but the relationship is far from perfectly inverse.

### Key Evidence

- **Negative correlation of –0.29** between monthly changes in JTSQUR and UNRATE (2001-02-01 to 2026-08-01) — statistically meaningful but not strong, indicating other forces also drive each series independently.
- **Current quits rate: 1.90%** (JTSQUR, 2026-08-01), measured as a percent of total employment, seasonally adjusted.
- **Current unemployment rate: 4.20%** (UNRATE, 2026-09-01), percent of labor force, seasonally adjusted.
- The intuition is sound: when workers feel confident enough to **voluntarily quit** (high quits rate), labor markets are typically tight and unemployment is low. Conversely, when unemployment rises, workers tend to stay put.

### Caveats
- The quits rate (JTSQUR) lags UNRATE by one month in the latest available data, so the most recent comparison is not perfectly synchronized.
- A correlation of –0.29 leaves most variation unexplained; both series are influenced by factors (e.g., sectoral shocks, policy changes) that don't affect the other.
- Both series are subject to revision.

## Housing Starts vs. Long-Term Rates: A Negative but Moderate Relationship Since 2022

**Bottom line:** Housing starts have declined meaningfully from their 2022 peak as 10-year Treasury yields surged to near-historic highs, but the relationship is weaker than might be expected, and starts remain broadly in line with pre-pandemic norms.

---

### Key Evidence

- **Rate surge is extreme:** The 10-year Treasury yield hit **5.31%** on 2026-10-05 (DGS10, 2026-10-05) — the highest in the 2018-to-present window — and was still at **5.22%** as of 2026-10-08 (DGS10, 2026-10-08), sitting at the **98th percentile** of its range since 2018, versus a series low of **0.52%** in August 2020.

- **Starts collapsed from their peak:** Housing starts peaked at **1,807 thousand units (SAAR)** in April 2022 (HOUST, 2022-04-01), right around when rate hikes began. The most recent reading is **1,275 thousand units** in August 2026 (HOUST, 2026-08-01) — a drop of roughly **532 thousand units, or ~29%** from that peak.

- **Starts are near the bottom of their post-2018 range:** At 1,275 thousand units, starts sit only **39% of the way** from the 2020 pandemic trough (936 thousand) to the 2022 peak (HOUST, 2026-08-01), signaling significant demand destruction relative to the boom years.

- **Correlation is negative but modest:** Month-over-month changes in housing starts and 10-year yields show a **–0.20 correlation** over 34 monthly observations from 2022 onward (HOUST/DGS10, 2022-03-01 to 2026-07-01). Rates are a headwind, but other factors (supply constraints, demographics, lock-in effect) cloud the signal.

- **Starts are still near pre-pandemic levels:** Despite the rate pressure, starts in August 2026 (1,275 thousand) are only **–1.3% below the 2019 average of 1,292 thousand** and **+2.2% above the 2017–2019 average of 1,248 thousand** (HOUST, 2026-08-01) — suggesting the market hasn't fully collapsed, just retreated from a frothy peak.

---

### Caveats
- **HOUST** is released with roughly a one-month lag and is subject to revision; the August 2026 figure is the latest available but may be revised.
- The –0.20 correlation uses **monthly changes** and covers only 34 observations — too few to draw strong causal conclusions.
- The 10-year Treasury is a benchmark rate, not a mortgage rate; the pass-through to 30-year mortgage rates (not retrieved here) may differ.
